statement: In the United States, alcohol was named on the death certificate in 14.7% of opioid overdose deaths in 2017 (12.4% in 1999; near 15% every year since 2008); in 2015–2017 the share was 15.0% of 122,940 deaths, 17.2% of men's and 10.5% of women's, similar in deaths involving heroin (16.5%), prescription opioids (14.2%) and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl (14.9%), lower with methadone (10.0%), and between 7.4% and 28.7% across states. Alcohol is under-recorded on death certificates, guidance on testing in opioid deaths does not address it, and reporting changed between states and years, so the true share is probably higher and the trend uncertain. Because the data contain nothing on how many people who use opioids also drink, they cannot show whether alcohol raises the risk of a fatal opioid overdose, or by how much; the correlation across states between binge drinking and the alcohol share of opioid deaths (r = 0.34) is an ecological association, not a finding about individuals.
plain: How often is alcohol involved in opioid overdose deaths? On US death certificates, alcohol was listed in about 15 of every 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share that has changed little since 2008. It was listed in about 17 in 100 men's deaths and about 10 in 100 women's, and at similar rates whether the opioid was heroin, a prescription opioid or fentanyl. Alcohol is often left off death certificates, so the real share is probably higher. These numbers show how often alcohol appears in opioid deaths; because the study did not know how many people drink while using opioids, it cannot say how much alcohol adds to the risk of dying.
population: All US opioid overdose deaths certified in 1999–2017 (399,230; 122,940 in 2015–2017), CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death data
exposure: Alcohol named among the multiple causes of death on the certificate (ICD-10 T51.0 ethanol or T51.9 alcohol unspecified)
comparator: None: shares among deaths (state-level comparisons only)
outcome: Share of opioid overdose deaths with alcohol co-involvement, by year, opioid type, sex and state
magnitude: Alcohol co-involvement in all US opioid overdose deaths: 12.4% (1999), near 15% since 2008, 14.7% (2017). 2015–2017: 18,419 of 122,940 (15.0%); men 14,178 of 82,506 (17.2%), women 4,241 of 40,434 (10.5%); heroin 7,245 of 43,940 (16.5%), methadone 984 of 9,868 (10.0%), prescription opioids 5,936 of 41,709 (14.2%), synthetic opioids 8,584 of 57,459 (14.9%); by state 7.4% (Mississippi) to 28.7% (District of Columbia), median 13.3%. In 2017, alcohol-involved deaths numbered 0.7 per 100,000 persons with heroin, 1.3 with synthetic opioids, 0.7 with prescription opioids and 0.1 with methadone. Death rates for alcohol-involved opioid overdoses rose 5.5-fold from 1999 to 2017, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. Ecological correlation of state binge-drinking prevalence with the alcohol share, 2015–2017: r = 0.34 (P = .02).

evidence.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 1 and 2 (images)
evidence.extracted: Alcohol co-involvement in all US opioid overdose deaths rose from 12.4% in 1999 to 14.7% in 2017 and stayed near 15% from 2008; death rates for alcohol-involved opioid overdoses rose 5.5-fold from 1999 to 2017 (all opioid overdose deaths 5.0-fold). By subtype: heroin 10.3%–20.1% over the period and 15.5% in 2017 (0.7 deaths per 100,000); synthetic opioids 11.5% in 2013 to 14.9% in 2017 (1.3 per 100,000); prescription opioids 14.3%–15.4% in 2007–2017 (0.7 per 100,000 in 2017); methadone below 10% until 2017 (0.1 per 100,000).

evidence.locator: Results › Current Co-involvement in 2015-2017 by Opioid Subtype, Sex, and State, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table
evidence.extracted: 2015–2017: alcohol named in 18,419 of 122,940 opioid overdose deaths (15.0%); men 17.2%, women 10.5%; heroin 16.5%, methadone 10.0%, prescription opioids 14.2%, synthetic opioids 14.9% (8,584 of 57,459); by state from 7.4% (Mississippi) to 28.7% (District of Columbia), median 13.3%; state alcohol and benzodiazepine shares uncorrelated (r = 0.08).

evidence.locator: Methods › Data Source, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Co-involvement is the mention of alcohol (T51.0 or T51.9) among the multiple causes on certificates of drug poisoning deaths with an opioid code. The authors state that alcohol is under-reported and often excluded from drug-related deaths, that the 2013 medical-examiner guidance does not address alcohol testing, that the 2006–2007 change in alcohol co-involvement may reflect 8 more states reporting and 481 extra alcohol-involved deaths reported by 8 others, that 12% of drug poisoning deaths in 2017 named no drug, that no individual-level data or blood levels were available, and that the counts are likely underestimated.

evidence.locator: Results › Association of Co-involvement With State-Level Binge Drinking and Benzodiazepine Prescribing, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Across states, self-reported binge-drinking prevalence (BRFSS) correlated with the alcohol share of opioid overdose deaths in 2015–2017, r = 0.34 (P = .02); South Dakota excluded for too few deaths. The authors state that the state-level correlations are not causal and may be prone to observational biases.

The authors report, from studies not read here, higher alcohol co-involvement with toxicology data: 22.3% of opioid deaths in Ontario, Canada (Gomes et al., 2017) and 18% alcohol-only co-intoxication in Massachusetts (Barocas et al., 2019); second-hand figures, cited only to show that certificate-based shares are lower.
evidence.quote: Alcohol remains an important and underrecognized cointoxicant in overdose deaths.

risk_of_bias.note: Under-recording of alcohol on death certificates, no alcohol testing guidance, and reporting that changed by state and year could change both the level and the trend materially (JBI moderate on the study card).

inconsistency.note: One data source; toxicology-based figures cited by the authors are higher, as expected from under-recording.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim describes certificate mentions in the United States and states what they do not show.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3) from one national death-certificate series; it starts low and is never upgraded. Risk of bias −1 for measurement (alcohol is under-recorded and testing and reporting changed over time and between states), so the shares are floors and the flat trend may partly reflect reporting. Inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision 0. Certainty very low for the exact share; the order of magnitude (about one in seven certified opioid deaths) is the study's finding. Status: single study. The claim states plainly that these data say nothing about how much alcohol raises the risk of dying: that needs individual-level studies with a denominator, none of which has been read.

verification.flag_note: No study read estimates the risk that alcohol adds to opioid overdose. Hickman et al. 2008 (Addiction, 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2008.02134.x) and White & Irvine 1999 (Addiction, 10.1046/j.1360-0443.1999.9479612.x), items 19 and 20 of the DOI list, are reviews of that question; Gomes et al. 2017 on alcohol in Ontario opioid deaths (Drug Alcohol Depend, 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2017.07.008) gives toxicology-based figures.
